title: Giorgio Agamben
keyWorks: Stanzas: Word and Phantasm in Western Culture (1977)
summary: Giorgio Agamben (b. 1942) is an Italian philosopher and a reader of Aristotle, Benjamin, Heidegger and medieval theologians. He writes short, almost poetic essays about how the modern world takes away our time, our attention and our free use of things — and how we can take them back. His key words are “profanation” (returning things to free use), “inoperativity” (liberation from the obligation to produce) and the “potential not to” (the freedom not to do what you are able to do).
onEmotions: Agamben doesn’t write textbooks about feelings, but his ideas shed a great deal of light on them. He observes that modern people are constantly captured by “apparatuses” — devices and arrangements (from schedules to the smartphone) that steer desires and behavior. Many of our heavy states — tiredness, overload, anxiety — are bound up with the demand to be always producing and always switched on. Agamben proposes not escape but “inoperativity” (Italian inoperosità): not laziness, but the capacity to suspend the obligation to deliver results and to see life as a possibility rather than a task. For him, a person is defined not only by what they can do but also by what they can not do — and in this “not” lie dignity and freedom.

anxiety.text: Anxiety makes sense: your thoughts run ahead, trying to live through everything that might happen in advance. In The Time That Remains, reflecting on the letters of the apostle Paul, Agamben distinguishes two ways of living time. One is an endless line along which we chase the future. The other is “the time that remains”: the contracted time we actually have, the present we live in rather than wait for. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that anxiety lives entirely in the first kind of time — a time that never arrives. There is no need to chase it away. But from time to time you can come back to the second: to this hour, this day, where the future has not yet taken the present from you.
anxiety.practice: Ask yourself: which of the things worrying me belong to this hour, and which to a time that hasn’t come yet? Sort them into two lists.

fear.text: Fear is a legitimate reaction to what is unclear and might threaten us. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben writes that you can only truly see your own time if you don’t look away from its darkness, not just from its lit-up places. And he adds: this takes courage. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that fear is often tied to our being afraid to look directly at what is dark. But the courage he speaks of is not fearlessness; it is the capacity to stay with what frightens you, without squeezing your eyes shut and without panicking. You don’t have to defeat fear all at once. You can try looking at it a little more closely — and discover that the darkness has contours.
fear.practice: Describe your fear in one concrete sentence: “I’m afraid that…” Try to name it more precisely than you usually do.

sadness.text: Sadness needs no justification. In his early book Stanzas, Agamben reconsiders the medieval idea of melancholy, long regarded as something like a vice. He shows that melancholy is bound up not with indifference but with desire: a person is sad because their desire is attached to something out of reach, and they go on holding on to it. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that your sadness is not emptiness but a form of faithfulness to what is dear to you. Sadness keeps a connection with what has slipped away. That doesn’t mean you have to stay in it forever. But you can treat it with respect: your capacity to love and to desire lives in it.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: what is my sadness reaching toward — what am I missing? Write it down in one word.

grief.text: Grief is a deep experience, and it needs time. In The Time That Remains, following Walter Benjamin, Agamben reflects on “the unforgettable.” Some lives and events, he writes, remain unforgettable even if no one in particular remembers them: what they ask of us is not so much to be remembered as to remain with us. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that what you have lost goes on belonging to the world, even when memory fades or pain makes remembering unbearable. You don’t have to hold everything in memory by effort in order to stay faithful. What was lost remains part of the world — and part of you — on its own.
grief.practice: If you want to, recall one small detail connected with the person or thing you have lost, and let it simply be with you for a while.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and it is not your fault. In The Coming Community, Agamben reflects on what a community of people might be like if it weren’t based on obligatory belonging — to a nation, a class, a group, “our own kind.” He speaks of “whatever” being: a person is valuable not because they have the right qualities but because they are such as they are. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that loneliness is often born of the feeling that we have to meet certain conditions in order to be accepted. But the genuine community he dreams of doesn’t require a pass. You already belong to the world — not by merit, but simply because you exist.
loneliness.practice: Recall a moment when you felt accepted without any conditions. Stay with that memory for a minute.

anger.text: Anger is legitimate and often points to a real injustice. In Profanations, Agamben describes how many things in the modern world end up removed from free use: time, space, language, the body are turned into resources that someone else controls. He calls returning things to people “profanation.” From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that anger often flares up where something has been taken from you — your time, your voice, your right to decide. Understanding this means not just seething but seeing exactly what you want to take back into your own free use. Then anger becomes not an explosion but a pointer. You don’t need to either muffle it or let it spill over — it is enough to understand what it is about.
anger.practice: Complete the sentence: “What was taken from me is…” And then: “What I would like to take back is…”

shame.text: Shame is one of the heaviest feelings, and it is hard to bear. In Remnants of Auschwitz, reflecting on the hardest testimonies of the twentieth century, Agamben, following Emmanuel Levinas, describes shame as the feeling of being delivered over to yourself, unable to hide from yourself. For Agamben, shame is not a sign of being rotten but something that reveals the very way of being human: we are at once those who act and those exposed to another’s gaze. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that shame speaks of your openness, not your worthlessness. You can live through this feeling without turning it into a verdict on yourself.
shame.practice: Notice whose gaze you feel ashamed before. Tell yourself: “This shame says that I am open, not that I am bad.”

guilt.text: Guilt shows that it matters to you how you acted. But Agamben offers an important distinction. In Remnants of Auschwitz, he writes that the concepts of guilt and responsibility come from law, while ethics is something else: not a trial of yourself but, as in Spinoza, a teaching about the happy life. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that endless self-accusation turns life into a court case in which you are both the accused and the prosecutor. That doesn’t mean actions don’t matter. But the ethical question is not “how guilty am I?” but “how do I want to live now?” This question opens the future, while the trial only keeps returning you to the past.
guilt.practice: Replace the question “how guilty am I?” with “how do I want to live after this?” and write down one answer.

envy.text: Envy is an understandable feeling, especially when it seems that others have what you don’t. In The Coming Community, Agamben reflects on what makes a person valuable. Usually we judge by properties: talents, successes, looks. Agamben suggests otherwise: value lies in “suchness” — in a person being exactly as they are, with all their properties, yet not reducible to any one of them. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that envy always compares properties. But your value is not the sum of your properties, and it can’t be measured against someone else’s. You are not a set of qualities slightly fewer than someone else’s, but the one and only way of being yourself.
envy.practice: Name one quality of yours that makes no sense to compare with anyone’s, because it is simply yours.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are a heavy state, when nothing brings joy and you don’t even feel like wanting anything. In Stanzas, Agamben reflects on the medieval notion of acedia — the despondency that monks called “the noonday demon.” It was considered a sin of sloth, but Agamben offers another reading: a person in acedia is not indifferent; their desire is still alive, but it is directed toward something that has become unreachable. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that even in emptiness there lives a hidden desire — it simply hasn’t found its way. Emptiness is not your absence but a waiting. There is no need to force interest into flame. You can simply acknowledge: somewhere inside, something is still reaching out.
emptiness.practice: Ask yourself: if I could want anything at all, what would it be? Write down the first thing that comes, even if it seems strange.

confusion.text: Confusion is natural when words and familiar explanations stop working. In Infancy and History, Agamben reflects on “infancy” in a special sense — the state before language, when we can’t yet name what we are experiencing. For him, this is not only a stage of life that has passed but a dimension a person returns to again and again: every time a new experience begins, we first find ourselves “without words.” From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that confusion is such a return to the infancy of experience. It is uncomfortable, but new understanding is born from it. There is no need to rush to explanations — words will come after the experience.
confusion.practice: Describe your state without using ready-made explanations: only what you see, feel and notice right now.

fatigue.text: Your tiredness is real, and it doesn’t mean you aren’t trying hard enough. In the essay “The Hunger of an Ox,” from the collection Nudities, Agamben reflects on the Sabbath and the feast. A feast, he writes, is not merely a break from work but a special state in which ordinary activities become “inoperative”: we eat not to restore our strength but for the sake of eating itself; we walk not to get somewhere but simply to stroll. Agamben calls this inoperativity (inoperosità) and sees in it not laziness but liberation from the obligation to produce. From his point of view, you might say: your tiredness is the voice of the part of you that wants not another break for the sake of work, but time that owes nothing to anyone.
fatigue.practice: Do one ordinary thing — drink some tea, take a walk — not for its usefulness or to recover, but simply for the sake of doing it.

boredom.text: Boredom can be agonizing, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. In The Open, Agamben turns to Heidegger’s reflections on “profound boredom.” In it, according to Heidegger, the things around us seem to refuse to occupy us — and in this very refusal a person first notices that their life is not just a set of activities but an open possibility. Agamben develops this thought: boredom brings us to the edge of habitual behavior, where we sense that we could be otherwise. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that boredom is not empty time but a time when the familiar has stopped holding us. You don’t have to drown it out; you can listen: what possibility is opening up in this “nothing is interesting”?
boredom.practice: Sit with your boredom for five minutes without filling it with your phone or tasks, and notice what comes to mind.

joy.text: Joy is wonderful, and it is worth living it fully. In “In Praise of Profanation,” from the collection Profanations, Agamben writes about children’s play: a child takes any object — an old toy car, a document, a key — and turns it into a plaything, freeing it from its former purpose. Play, for Agamben, returns things to a free, light kind of use. From his point of view, you might say that joy often resembles such play: for a while, things and activities stop being obligations and become simply something to enjoy. Joy doesn’t have to be earned or justified. You can let yourself play with the moment without turning it into a task.
joy.practice: Notice what in this joy is like play: what you are doing right now not for a result, but just because.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most important feelings. In The Coming Community, Agamben writes that love is not directed at particular qualities of the beloved: their beauty, intelligence or kindness. But neither does it disregard them: the lover wants the other with all their properties — such as they are. Agamben calls this “whatever” being: not “it doesn’t matter which,” but such that all of it matters. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that love is the experience of another person in their “suchness.” And perhaps it is in love that we ourselves first feel accepted not for something, but whole.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and name something in them that you love not for its usefulness or merit, but simply because it is them.

quote.text: The coming being is whatever being.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling in which the world seems generous. In the essay “Magic and Happiness,” from Profanations, Agamben writes that true happiness is never a reward for merit: what we achieve through our own efforts brings a different kind of joy, while happiness comes like magic — as a gift, unearned. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that gratitude is the recognition of such a gift. You have received something that could not have been earned — and it is not a debt to be repaid but a reason for joy. Gratitude frees you from the bookkeeping of merit: you can simply accept the good without asking whether you deserve it, and be glad that the world is sometimes generous.
gratitude.practice: Name one good thing in your life that you didn’t earn — it simply happened. Silently give thanks for it.

hope.text: Hope is precious, especially when things are hard. In The Coming Community, Agamben retells a parable that Walter Benjamin heard from Gershom Scholem: in the world to come, everything will be as it is now, just a little different. There is no need to destroy everything and build it anew — a small displacement that changes everything is enough. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that hope doesn’t require the promise of a complete transformation. It can rest on tiny changes that are possible already: a slightly different way of looking, a slightly different place for things. The better may not be far away — it may be just a small shift away. Such hope is modest, but that is exactly why it is hard to take away.
hope.practice: Think of one small thing in your life that could become “just a little different.” Do it today.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender longing for the past, and there is nothing shameful in it. In Stanzas, Agamben offers a bold thought about melancholy: it is not simply a reaction to a real loss but a remarkable capacity of the imagination to make something unreachable present — even if as something lost. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that nostalgia often longs not only for what was, but for what never was exactly as it is remembered. This is not deception but the creative work of memory: this is how we hold on to what is dear to us. You can value nostalgia as a way of keeping a connection with what shaped you, without demanding that the past come back.
nostalgia.practice: Recall what you miss, and ask: what exactly am I keeping in this memory — a place, a time, or a feeling?

craving.text: A craving can be very strong, and it is not your fault that it comes. In the essay “What Is an Apparatus?”, Agamben describes devices and arrangements — from schedules to the smartphone — that capture our gestures and desires. He pays particular attention to how the phone reshapes a person’s behavior. From his point of view, you might say that a craving is a moment when your desire is being steered by something from outside: a habit, a device, a substance. Agamben proposes “profanation” — returning things and gestures to free use. You might try noticing the craving without giving in to it right away: it rises and falls, like a wave. Each such pause is a small return of freedom to yourself.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, wait a few minutes and watch how it changes. Ask: who is doing the wanting right now — me, or the habit?

quote.text: If to consecrate (sacrare) was the term that designated the removal of things from the sphere of human law, to profane meant, conversely, to return them to the free use of men.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure. It is a loop that has become fixed and organized a life around itself, and getting out of it is hard. In “In Praise of Profanation,” Agamben distinguishes “use” from “consumption”: to use a thing is to have a free, living relationship with it; to consume means the thing is swallowed up, and the person is captured by its logic. From his point of view, you might say that addiction is a place where free use has turned into compulsion. It isn’t about weakness of character: Agamben shows that much of modern life is designed to capture us. Getting your freedom back is a long road, and you don’t have to walk it alone.
addiction.practice: Write down what this habit frees you from for a while — what it stands in for. If you like, think of a person, or a mutual-help group, where you could talk about it.

hangover.text: The morning after can be very hard: feeling unwell, anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. This is no reason to punish yourself. In The Coming Community, Agamben writes that a person is not the sum of separate acts but a “manner,” a way of being: how they live, not only what they have done. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that last night is not the final definition of you. Your way of being includes this morning too: how you treat yourself now. There is no need to put yourself on trial. You can simply get through this morning gently, taking care of yourself the way you would care for someone close to you.
hangover.practice: Write down three simple things you can do today to take care of yourself — as you would for someone you love.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid, powerful state when everything seems possible. There is no need to spoil it. In the essay “Magic and Happiness,” Agamben writes that true happiness comes not as a deserved reward but as magic — unexpectedly, unearned. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that euphoria feels exactly like this: as if a door you weren’t looking for had opened. Agamben also reminds us that human power includes the “potential not to” — not everything that is possible in this moment has to be done right away. This doesn’t cool the euphoria; it lets you live it more fully: to enjoy what has opened up without turning every sense of possibility into an obligation.
euphoria.practice: Write down one thing that seems possible right now, and let it simply be a dream, without immediately turning it into a plan.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid moment — is very unpleasant, and it makes sense. In the essay “The Hunger of an Ox,” Agamben writes that a feast is not a separate time set against everyday life but a special way of living ordinary activities: eating, talking, walking not for their usefulness but just because. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the comedown is often sharper when the feast seems like an exception and everyday life like a gray duty. But you can gradually carry the festive into ordinary life. The drop doesn’t mean everything good is over. It can become a time when you learn to find grains of celebration in the simplest things.
crash.practice: Find one small action in today that you can do not for its usefulness, but as a little celebration.

panic.text: Panic is a very frightening experience: a wave of terror, a pounding heart, the feeling that something irreparable is about to happen. Your fear makes sense. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. In “Notes on Gesture,” Agamben writes of the gesture as an action that produces nothing and leads nowhere — pure movement. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that in panic the mind feverishly tries to understand what is happening and paints a catastrophe. Simple gestures with no goal — an out-breath, touching the floor, looking at an object — help you return to your body without solving anything. You don’t need to understand anything. It is enough to wait out the wave.
panic.practice: Place your feet on the floor and feel the support. Take a few slow breaths, letting each out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, and name aloud three objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is all this for,” the sense of an abyss — is one of the hardest feelings. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben offers an unexpected view of darkness. He points out that, according to neurophysiology, darkness is not simply the absence of light: there are special cells in the eye that actively “produce” it. Seeing darkness is also an activity. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that your dread is not blindness but a way of seeing what others don’t notice. It takes courage, but there is dignity in this way of looking too. The darkness you are looking at is not the end of meaning but the place where the question of meaning begins.
dread.practice: Write down your “what for” question in one sentence — not to answer it, but to see it clearly.

quote.text: The contemporary is he who firmly holds his gaze on his own time so as to perceive not its light, but rather its darkness.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

fomo.text: The fear of missing out makes sense: it feels as though life is happening somewhere you are not. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben reflects on fashion. Fashion, he writes, always lives in a “now” that can’t be grasped: as soon as you are “in fashion,” you are already almost out of it. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the fear of missing out is a chase after this elusive “now,” which by its very nature can’t be caught. But Agamben also says something else: the truly contemporary person is one who doesn’t fully coincide with their time and keeps a little distance. Being “not there” is not a failure but the condition for seeing clearly what is going on.
fomo.practice: Name one thing you’re afraid of missing, and ask: do I actually want this, or am I afraid of being “out of fashion”?

sleepless.text: Insomnia is agonizing, and night thoughts feel heavier than daytime ones. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that at three in the morning the mind keeps working — trying to solve problems, draw conclusions, make plans — as if even the night were obliged to deliver results. Agamben calls liberation from the obligation to produce “inoperativity” (inoperosità). The night hours don’t have to be productive, or even rest in the strict sense. You don’t have to solve your thoughts; you can simply let them go by without taking part. This isn’t a cure for insomnia, but it removes an extra weight — the feeling that you have to do something with this night.
sleepless.practice: Tell yourself: “Tonight I don’t have to solve anything.” Write your thoughts in a notebook, one line each, and leave them until morning.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: a trust that seemed solid collapses. In The Sacrament of Language: An Archaeology of the Oath, Agamben shows that the oath — an ancient attempt to guarantee that words will match deeds — was bound up from the very beginning with the possibility of breaking it. An oath is needed precisely because a word can turn out to be untrue. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that betrayal is not proof of your naivety. Trust was always a risk, and you took it because there is no closeness without trust. The pain of betrayal is the price of that courage, not evidence of a mistake. Your capacity to trust is not broken — it is wounded, and it needs time.
betrayal.practice: Write: “I trusted because…” — and acknowledge that this trust was a brave act, not foolishness.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is an agonizing feeling in which love and the fear of loss are mixed. In The Highest Poverty, Agamben reflects on the Franciscans, who renounced property but not the use of things: living with things without owning them. He sees in this an image of a different relationship to the world — use without appropriation. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that jealousy is an attempt to turn love into property, to hold on to a person as a possession. But closeness, like Franciscan “poverty,” can be a bond without appropriation. This doesn’t mean giving up the feeling — it means asking what a love might be like that doesn’t hold on but shares.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: what do I want — to possess this person or to be close to them? Write down what the difference is for you.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is heavy, and as a rule it speaks of a real injustice. The Coming Community has a short chapter called “Irreparable.” Agamben writes that things are as they are — delivered over to their way of being with no possibility of correction. That sounds grim, but he sees in it a source of liberation: acknowledging the irreparable frees us from the endless attempt to rewrite the past. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that resentment keeps an unfinished trial going inside — as if the past could still be put right if you remember the wrong long enough. Acknowledging that it was the way it was doesn’t mean justifying it. It means no longer spending your life on a trial that can never end.
resentment.practice: Write one sentence: “It was the way it was” — and notice what changes in your body as you say it.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart really hurts. In Idea of Prose, Agamben describes love as living in intimacy with something foreign — not in order to appropriate it or make it fully understandable, but to preserve its otherness. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that a breakup lays bare what was true before as well: the other person never fully belonged to you; they always remained themselves. That is bitter, but there is consolation in it too: what you loved was real precisely because it was other, not a copy of you. Your love was not a mistake — it was an encounter with someone other that changed you.
heartbreak.practice: Name one thing you learned about the other person in this relationship that surprised you with its difference from you.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out is familiar to a great many people. In the essay “Nudity,” Agamben reflects on what we imagine lies beneath clothing — as if some secret were hidden there, a shameful truth. But for Agamben, being unclothed reveals nothing of the kind: behind the clothing there is no hidden essence, only a “this” — the body as it is. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that impostor syndrome lives on the same fear: as if a shameful truth were hidden behind your work. But behind your deeds there is no secret “really, I’m nobody.” There is you — as you are, doing what you do. There is nothing to expose.
impostor.practice: Write: “If I’m ‘found out,’ they’ll see that I…” — and finish it honestly. Often it turns out to be simply a person who is learning.

self_hatred.text: If your inner voice says cruel things about you, that is very hard, and you deserve to be treated with care. In The Coming Community, in the short chapter on ethics, Agamben writes that there is no essence a human being must embody, no destiny they must fulfil. That is precisely why ethics is possible at all. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the inner critic compares you with an ideal that doesn’t actually exist — with the “right” you that you supposedly should have become. But there is no such standard. You haven’t failed your destiny, because there wasn’t one. You are a possibility, not a failed project.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic, and next to it: “I don’t have to match a template that doesn’t exist.”

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is very hard, and it often reflects real circumstances. Agamben reflects a great deal on Aristotle’s thought that human potential always includes the potential not to: whoever can play the flute can also not play. Impotence, for Agamben, is not simply a lack of power but part of human potential. From his point of view, you might say that even when you can’t change your circumstances, you don’t turn into a thing: your capacity to choose your attitude, to notice, to wait remains. This is not a promise of change. It is a recognition that even in powerlessness you remain alive, not a broken mechanism.
helplessness.practice: Name one thing you can do or not do right now — even the smallest. Notice that there is still a choice.

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is agonizing, and it isn’t laziness. In the essay “Bartleby, or On Contingency,” Agamben examines Herman Melville’s story about a scrivener who answers every request with: “I would prefer not to.” For Agamben, Bartleby is a figure of the “potential not to”: a person can not only do but also not do, and therein lies their freedom. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that procrastination is a spontaneous expression of this potential, which we experience as guilt. But it is important to ask: what exactly in me wants to say “I would prefer not to”? Sometimes it is a protest against the task, sometimes tiredness, sometimes fear. Once you hear it, it is easier to find where to begin.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: “What in me would prefer not to do this — and why?” Write down the answer in one sentence.

quote.author: Herman Melville
quote.source: “Bartleby, the Scrivener” (Agamben devoted his essay “Bartleby, or On Contingency” to this phrase)

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home is a profound experience: the ground beneath you, your language, your familiar ties all slip away. In the essay “Beyond Human Rights,” following Hannah Arendt, Agamben reflects on the figure of the person who has left their country. He suggests that this is not an exception to the rule but perhaps one of the central figures of our time: more and more people live between places and languages. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that you haven’t fallen out of normal life — you are living an experience that says a great deal about the modern world. His “coming community” is a community that doesn’t require a single shared soil. You can belong without being “from here.”
uprooted.practice: Name one person in your new place with whom you are connected not by origin but by something else. What is it?

overload.text: Overload is real: the endless feed and the noise are draining. In Infancy and History, Agamben observes that modern people come home in the evening worn out by a multitude of events — and not one of them has become experience. We are flooded with impressions, but they don’t add up to anything lived through. In the essay “On What We Can Not Do,” he adds: we have lost touch with our “potential not to,” and so we believe we must cope with everything. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that your overload is not an inability but a sign that you have been deprived of the right not to take things in. Reclaiming your “not” means beginning to have experience again.
overload.practice: Choose one feed or notification and switch it off for an hour. Tell yourself: “I can not know this right now.”

quote.text: Separated from his impotentiality, deprived of the experience of what he can not do, today’s man believes himself capable of everything.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben
quote.source: “On What We Can Not Do,” Nudities

unreality.text: The feeling that nothing is quite real is frightening and disorienting. It deserves to be described gently. Continuing Guy Debord’s idea of “the society of the spectacle,” Agamben writes about a world in which reality increasingly turns into images and pictures, and language and experience are separated from us. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the sense of unreality partly echoes this era: you are not making it up out of nothing. But Agamben also sees a chance in it — to see what is usually hidden behind familiarity. Unreality can be gently balanced by what is simple and tangible, what can’t be turned into a picture.
unreality.practice: Touch three objects with different textures and say aloud what each one feels like. Do it slowly.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious state. In the essay “What Is the Contemporary?”, Agamben offers an image that evokes exactly this feeling. The night sky is dark because the light of distant galaxies, moving away from us, travels toward us but cannot reach us. To see in the darkness this light that is striving toward us — that is what it means to be contemporary. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that awe is the experience of something that exceeds our capacity to take it in and yet touches us. It doesn’t need explaining. You can simply let yourself be the one the light reaches.
awe.practice: Look at something large — the sky, a tree, the horizon — and stay with it for a minute, doing nothing.

relief.text: Relief is a wonderful feeling, when something that was pressing on you lets go. It is worth living it. In The Time That Remains, Agamben reads Paul’s “as not” — living in your roles and duties as though they don’t hold you entirely. The roles remain, but they lose their power over you. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that relief is the moment when one of these roles or duties suddenly loosens its grip: you are still the same person, but you no longer have to hold on to it with all your strength. You can savor relief and remember it as a reminder: not every burden has to rest on you forever.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and name what you have just been freed from. Let your shoulders drop.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and worth protecting. For Agamben, inoperativity (inoperosità) is neither emptiness nor laziness but a special state in which life is not subordinated to a task. He gives the example of poetry: it takes language, which usually serves to convey messages, and lets it simply sound. In The Coming Community he also speaks of “ease” (Italian agio) — the free space beside a thing where it can move. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that calm is this kind of ease: you are doing nothing useful, yet living more fully. Calm doesn’t need to be turned into rest for the sake of new tasks. It is good in itself.
calm.practice: Sit for five minutes doing nothing, without turning it into a practice “for the sake of something.” Simply be.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful state, when you want to create. In the essay “Genius,” from Profanations, Agamben recalls that the ancient Romans believed each person has their own Genius — a god born together with them. For Agamben, Genius is the impersonal part of us, something greater than our “I” that doesn’t entirely belong to us. From his point of view, you might say that inspiration is an encounter with this part. You don’t produce inspiration through effort; it comes as if you were living alongside someone strange and generous. You don’t need to appropriate or control it. You can simply follow it for as long as it leads.
inspiration.practice: Write down whatever comes, without editing — as if you were taking dictation from someone else.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — the small pleasure in someone else’s failure — is familiar to almost everyone, and people are usually ashamed of it. In itself it says little about who you are. Continuing Guy Debord’s idea of “the society of the spectacle,” Agamben writes about a world in which life increasingly becomes a show: we watch other people’s successes and failures like images in a shop window, where everyone is constantly being compared. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that schadenfreude is the feeling of a spectator at this spectacle. When someone else’s life becomes a picture in a ranking, their fall briefly lifts us a rung higher. Simply noticing that you have ended up in the role of spectator is already freeing: behind the picture a living person shows through again — and so does your own weariness with the race.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, ask yourself: what competition am I taking part in right now — and did I choose it?

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold look from above, and it often serves as protection: against disappointment, powerlessness, fear. Feeling it is human. In The Open, Agamben describes what he calls the “anthropological machine”: the way a culture again and again defines the “true human” by separating off those declared “lower,” almost animal. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that contempt is a small, personal version of this machine: it draws a line with “us” on one side and those who are beneath us on the other. Agamben proposes stopping the machine — not drawing a new line but suspending the division itself. You don’t need to force yourself to respect someone you despise. But you can notice the line you are drawing and ask what it protects in you.
contempt.practice: Complete the sentence: “In despising this person, I am separating myself from…” — and listen to the answer.

disgust.text: Disgust is a very bodily feeling: toward a situation, toward people, sometimes toward yourself. The body recoils before thought does, and there is nothing to be ashamed of here. In his essay on taste, Agamben reflects that taste is a special kind of knowledge: it doesn’t prove anything but distinguishes the pleasant from the unpleasant immediately, with the body. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that disgust is the dark side of this capacity: the body’s instant knowledge of what it doesn’t want to let in. It isn’t always right, but it always tells you something. If disgust is directed at yourself, it is worth recalling Agamben’s thought from The Coming Community: a person is not a sum of properties that can be taken away or rejected, but a way of being. What seems “vile” in you is not the whole truth about you.
disgust.practice: Notice what your body is recoiling from and name it in one word. Then ask: is this knowledge about the world, or about my tiredness?

revenge.text: The wish for revenge makes sense: you have been hurt, and you want the person who hurt you to pay. It doesn’t make you cruel — it speaks to the depth of the wound. In his short book Karman, Agamben explores how Western thought linked action, guilt and punishment into a single chain: every act gives rise to a debt that must be paid. He doubts that this bookkeeping exhausts ethics. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that revenge lives by the same logic: the account stays open until the pain has been returned. But such a chain rarely ends — it only passes from one person to the next. Acknowledging your wish for revenge is honest. Asking what would really give you back your footing means stepping out of the bookkeeping, without giving up on justice or on protecting yourself.
revenge.practice: Write: “The account I’m keeping open is…” And then: “What I really need is…”

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — can be sharp, and then shame arrives. But it doesn’t cancel love. In “In Praise of Profanation,” Agamben writes that everything declared sacred is removed from ordinary life: it can’t be touched, it can’t be freely used. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that family roles, too, sometimes become such “sacred” images: the perfect mother, the grateful son, the flawless partner. They are not allowed to be angry or tired. Anger at someone close is sometimes a clumsy profanation of these roles: a return of the relationship to ordinary, living, imperfect life. This is no reason to hurt the people you love. But it is a reason to forgive yourself for being a living person and not an icon.
anger_at_loved.practice: Name one “sacred” role you carry in your family, and complete the sentence: “In this role I’m not allowed to…”

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a tangled feeling, and it seems you must decide which of the two is true. Agamben reflects a great deal on Aristotle’s thought that every potential is at once a potential to be and a potential not to be, to do and not to do. One doesn’t exist without the other. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that closeness works the same way: the capacity to love someone is inseparable from the capacity to pull away, be irritated, disagree. Ambivalence is not a breakdown of love but a sign that it is alive and free rather than compelled. A love without the possibility of “not” would be more like a duty. You can let both feelings be, without demanding an immediate choice of yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Write: “I can love you and I can not stand you — and both are mine.” Stay with this sentence for a while.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a seriously ill loved one often comes together with shame. But relief and love can live side by side. In Opus Dei, Agamben traces how the notion of duty, of service, of “office” gradually became the main model of ethics: to live is to carry out an obligation. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that long care for a loved one or a hard relationship turns life into just such an endless service, with no room for anything but the function. Relief is the moment when the service is over and life can once again simply be life. This doesn’t cancel the love that was inside that service. Your relief is not a betrayal but a release from a burden you carried because you loved.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: “My service is over, and the love remains.” Notice what happens in your body.

indifference.text: Sometimes something happens that “should” move you — and inside it is quiet, and on top of that comes worry: “Am I heartless?” In his first book, The Man Without Content, Agamben reflects on the modern spectator: more and more, we look at the world from the outside, as if at an exhibition, and precisely for that reason it less and less truly grips us. In Infancy and History he adds that modern people live through many events that never become experience. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that your indifference is not a personal flaw but a shared affliction of an era that buries us in impressions and robs us of the time to live through them. Your feelings haven’t disappeared — they simply had nowhere to enter. Perhaps they need quiet and slowing down.
indifference.practice: Choose one event from the past few days and calmly stay with it for two minutes — without your phone, simply recalling the details.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and leave can be very strong. It is legitimate: this is often how something speaks that has long been given no room. In the essay “What Is an Apparatus?”, Agamben describes how modern life is saturated with apparatuses — schedules, rules, positions, gadgets — that capture our gestures and desires. He notes that you can’t simply run away from apparatuses: new ones appear everywhere. But you can “profane” them — take back free use of what has been captured. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the wish to run away is a sign that you have felt this capture. Whether to leave or not is for you alone to decide. But first you can notice which part of your life you want to take back, wherever you end up.
escape.practice: Complete the sentence: “What has been taken from me most is…” — and think about what small piece of it you could take back as soon as this week.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off limits” often brings turmoil, as if the feeling itself were already a transgression. But attraction doesn’t ask permission, and it says little about your integrity. In Stanzas, Agamben examines the medieval theory of love, according to which one loves not simply a person but their image — a “phantasm” that the imagination keeps and cherishes within. The poets of that time knew that love largely converses with this inner image. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that attraction to someone unavailable is often especially strong precisely because the image has no limits: reality doesn’t argue with it. That doesn’t make the feeling false. But you can ask with curiosity: what exactly lives in this image — and what does it say about you yourself?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Describe in three words the image of this person that lives in your imagination. Then ask: what does this image want in me?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment — the stiffness, the burning face, the wish to become invisible — is exhausting, and you are not alone in it. In the short essay “The Face,” Agamben writes that the face is above all openness: the place where a person is exposed to others and cannot escape it. We all try to cope with this exposure — we hide behind roles, masks, expressions. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that social anxiety is an acute experience of this shared openness. But it isn’t peculiar to you: everyone in the room is just as exposed, just as vulnerable. Agamben even saw in this shared openness a basis for human community. Your vulnerability is not a defect but the very thing that connects you with others.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, tell yourself: “Everyone here is just as open as I am.” And take one slow breath out.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty — not knowing what will happen — is hard: the mind tries again and again to calculate everything. Agamben thinks a great deal about the “contingent” in the old philosophical sense: contingent is what can be and can also not be. We are used to seeing a threat in this. But for Agamben, contingency is the condition of freedom: in a world where everything was necessary and predetermined, there would be no room for either choice or hope. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that uncertainty is a world in which possibility is still at work. That doesn’t cancel the anxiety: not knowing is hard. But you can remember that an open future is not only a space of bad outcomes. It also holds ones you haven’t thought of yet.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “This could turn out one way or another.” Add one possibility that would make you glad.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — is wearing: time stretches out, and life seems to be put on pause. In The Time That Remains, Agamben reads the apostle Paul and speaks of “messianic time.” It is not a distant end to be waited out but a time within time: a special, contracted “now” in which we already live. For Agamben, what matters in it is not what comes afterward but how we live this interval. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that waiting is not empty time that you simply have to endure. Even when the outcome isn’t in your hands, the interval belongs to you. You can live it, not just sit it out.
waiting.practice: Set aside thoughts about the outcome for two minutes and do something wholly in the present: make some tea, look out of the window.

quote.text: Messianic time is the time that time takes to come to an end.
quote.author: Giorgio Agamben

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can keep coming back for years: “if only I had…” This feeling shows what mattered to you. In the essay “Bartleby, or On Contingency,” Agamben recalls a thought of Walter Benjamin’s: remembrance can make the incomplete complete, and the complete incomplete. For Agamben, memory doesn’t simply store the past; it gives it back its possibility: what was opens up anew — as something that could have been otherwise. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that regret is a painful form of this kind of memory: you see possibilities in the past that were never realized. They can’t be brought back, but they can be acknowledged. Sometimes what didn’t happen then can find another, new place in your life now.
regret.practice: Name one possibility you missed back then, and ask: in what small form could it live now?

longing.text: Longing for a particular person can be almost physical: you miss their voice, their gaze, their presence. This feeling is legitimate. In Nymphs, following the art historian Aby Warburg, Agamben writes about the “afterlife” of images: images are not dead; they are charged with time and go on living, returning, stirring us. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the image of someone you love within you is not a pale copy but a living, charged image: it comes in dreams, in the chance gestures of passers-by, in smells. Longing is an encounter with such an image when the person themselves is not near. It hurts, but it also keeps the connection. You don’t have to fight this image; you can let it live in you.
longing.practice: Let yourself remember this person for a minute in one specific scene — with its light, sounds and details.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — hard news, wars, injustice — can overwhelm you so much that it is hard to live your own life. This pain is legitimate. In Remnants of Auschwitz, Agamben reflects on testimony: on how hard and how important it is to listen to those who have survived terrible things, and not to turn away from the unbearable. He writes that complete testimony is impossible: the most terrible things always remain unspoken. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that your pain is a form of bearing witness: you don’t look away. But a witness doesn’t have to bear everything alone. You can listen, remember, name — and still give yourself pauses. Being faithful to the world doesn’t require you to be destroyed along with it.
world_pain.practice: Choose one thing from what you saw today that you want to remember. Then put the news aside and do something caring for yourself.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds painfully: it feels as though a verdict has been passed on you. This pain is real. Following Aristotle, Agamben says that every potential includes the “potential not to”: whoever can do something can also not do it. In this possibility of refusal he sees the essence of human freedom. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that another person’s “no” is an expression of their freedom, their “potential not to,” and not a measure of your worth. They could have said “yes,” they could have said “no” — and they chose “no” for their own reasons, which are not always about you. In The Coming Community, Agamben insists that a person is valuable not for a set of properties someone has approved or rejected, but for their very way of being.
rejection.practice: Write: “Their ‘no’ is about their freedom. My worth hasn’t changed because of it.” Read it again slowly.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be tenacious: any silence from someone close seems like the beginning of the end. Behind this fear is a real need for a secure connection. In The Coming Community, Agamben dreams of a community that doesn’t require a person to earn belonging, meet conditions, or prove they are “one of us.” From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the fear of abandonment often lives by the logic of conditions: “they’ll leave me if I turn out not to be enough…” Agamben proposes seeing a person as “whatever” being — valuable not for meeting requirements but simply as it is. This doesn’t guarantee that no one will ever leave. But it reminds you: your worth doesn’t depend on whether people stay with you.
abandonment.practice: Complete the sentence: “I’m afraid they’ll leave me if I…” — and notice what condition you have set for yourself.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts in a special way: the feeling is enormous, and there is no answer. In Stanzas, Agamben explains that the Italian word stanza means “dwelling,” “room”: poets used it for the essential part of a poem, which holds love like a home. Medieval love poetry was often born of love that received no answer — and it was this poetry that created such “rooms” for it. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that unrequited love is not wasted: it needs a place where it can live without demanding an answer. That place can be a letter, poems, a diary, music, or simply an inner room. You can grieve what didn’t come true — and still give your feeling a home rather than driving it out.
unrequited.practice: Write a few lines about your love, without addressing the person and without planning to send them. Let it have a “room” of its own.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: it is as if you had been stripped of your place among people. The blame for this does not lie with you. In Remnants of Auschwitz, Agamben points out that the Latin dignitas — “dignity” — originally meant rank, office, standing in society. Dignity of this kind can be taken away, the way someone is removed from office. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that humiliation strikes precisely at this “dignity as rank”: at the place others assign to you. But a person does not coincide with their role and mask. In The Coming Community, Agamben speaks of the human being as a way of being that can’t be reduced to a position or an assessment. Humiliation wounds — but what in you runs deeper than any role cannot be taken from you.
humiliation.practice: Write: “They tried to take from me…, but what remains in me is…” — and name something that doesn’t depend on anyone else’s gaze.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background, and behind it lies real pressure — advertising, comparisons, other people’s remarks. In his late book The Use of Bodies, Agamben proposes thinking of the body not as property to be appraised like an item on the market but through “use”: a living relationship in which we not only use the body but are ourselves affected by it. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that body shame arises when the body turns into a shop window, an object to be judged from outside. In use, the body is what you live with: you walk, embrace, taste food, feel warmth. You may not love every feature and still give your body back its life — from the inside, not from the mirror.
body_shame.practice: Make one movement simply for the sensation — stretch, take a few steps, warm your hands — and notice how your body lives from the inside.

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, is a hard experience: it is frightening, painful, and it seems you are being reduced to a diagnosis. These feelings are legitimate. Agamben speaks of “form-of-life” — a life that cannot be separated from its form: from its way of living, feeling, looking at the world. He criticizes the habit of dividing a person into “bare” biological life and everything else. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that even in illness you are not just an organism with symptoms but a whole form of life: your attachments, habits, your way of seeing. Illness changes this form but doesn’t cancel it. You can take care of your body and at the same time protect what makes your life yours — small things, conversations, things you love.
illness.practice: Name one thing that makes your life yours and that has stayed with you despite the illness.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, well-earned feeling, and there is no need to hide it. In Infancy and History, Agamben writes that modern people live through many events but rarely a real experience: something truly lived, understood and made their own. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that healthy pride is a rare moment of exactly this kind of experience. You did something, and it isn’t just an item on a to-do list — it has become part of you. Agamben also values the “potential not to”: part of your pride may also be about what you managed to turn down in order to do what mattered most. You can let yourself be fully glad, without rushing on to the next task.
pride.practice: Tell yourself — aloud or in writing — the story of what you did in three sentences: the beginning, the difficulty, the result.

melancholy.text: A bright sadness, melancholy, is a quiet, slightly sad and yet warm state. It doesn’t need fixing. In Stanzas, Agamben examines Albrecht Dürer’s engraving Melencolia I in detail: a pensive winged figure sits among scattered tools and objects that have lost their usual purpose. From Agamben’s point of view, you might say that the melancholy gaze sees things differently: not as means to an end but as if for the first time — in their strangeness and beauty. It is no accident that melancholy has long been associated with contemplation and creativity. A bright sadness lets you see the familiar as precious and fragile. You can simply stay in it for a while, letting the things around you become a little more meaningful.
melancholy.practice: Choose an object near you and look at it for a minute as if it weren’t needed for anything — as if it simply is.
